reflections.title: "I Will Show You Kindness"

reflect.text: When David called Mephibosheth, he told him not to be afraid. He promised to restore all the land of his grandfather Saul and invited him to eat at the royal table always. Mephibosheth had done nothing to earn this special favor, and he had no great deeds to offer. David acted purely out of faithfulness to a promise he had made years before to Jonathan. As F. B. Meyer explains, David was fulfilling a "sacred obligation" that provided for Jonathan's family.

David showed that keeping his word was far more important than wealth or past rivalries. It takes humility and intentional effort to overcome suspicion and restore broken relationships. In a similar way, we cannot earn our seat at God's table. We receive His welcome because of the covenant between the Father and the Son. When we receive God's generous love, we are also called to humble ourselves and show that same faithful kindness to others.

questions: Are there promises you need to keep or relationships where you need to take the first step to show kindness?
How does knowing God accepts you through Jesus, rather than your own efforts, take away your fear?
reflections.prayer: Heavenly Father, thank You for welcoming us through the covenant of Your Son, Jesus. Help us to rest in Your unfailing love instead of trying to earn Your favor. Give us humble hearts so that we can keep our promises and show generous kindness to others. Amen.

reflections.title: "A Dead Dog Like Me"

reflect.text: When Mephibosheth heard David's offer, he bowed down and called himself a dead dog. In the ancient world, kings usually executed the relatives of former rulers to protect their own thrones. Mephibosheth knew he had no claim to the king's favor and had nothing to offer. His deep humility reflects our own spiritual condition before God. We have no righteousness of our own to earn God's welcome, and the more we understand His grace, the more we realize our unworthiness.

Grace, God's kindness that we do not deserve, acts like light that reveals who we truly are. As Charles Spurgeon wrote, "grace, like light, reveals our impurity." We are frail and marked by sin, yet the Lord seeks out fearful sinners to bring them into His family. Even though Mephibosheth felt worthless, he still had to accept David's invitation. God freely offers His adopting love to us, and in humble faith, we can step forward and receive it.

questions: Why does understanding God's grace make us feel more humble rather than proud?
Have you accepted God's invitation to be part of His family, or are you holding back out of fear?
reflections.prayer: Lord God, we know we bring nothing of our own to earn Your favor. Thank You for seeking us out in our weakness and offering us a place in Your family. Teach us to walk in genuine humility and to gladly receive Your free gift of grace through faith. Amen.

reflections.title: "At the King's Table"

reflect.text: Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem and ate daily at David's table, even though he was lame in both feet. He was not a strong or impressive figure, but his weakness did not disqualify him from royal honor. David looked on him with love because of his covenant with Jonathan. In the same way, God welcomes us to His table because of Christ. As Charles Spurgeon noted, "lameness is no bar to sonship." Our physical weaknesses or struggles do not take away our place in God's family.

David showed true biblical kindness, which is steadfast covenant love shown through sacrificial action. Even after reaching the height of royal power, David did not forget his promise, nor did he overlook Saul's grandson. Instead, he treated someone from an enemy's household like his own son. This gracious love reminds us of how Jesus gave His life to save those who were once His enemies. Because we have received such steadfast mercy, we are called to show practical compassion to the weak and vulnerable who can never repay us.

questions: How does knowing that weakness is no barrier to being God's child encourage you today?
Who is someone vulnerable or overlooked in your life that you can serve without expecting anything back?
reflections.prayer: Heavenly Father, thank You that our weakness does not shut us out from Your presence and love. Thank You for welcoming us as Your children for Jesus' sake. Give us hearts that look out for the vulnerable and show steadfast kindness to those in need. Amen.

D4.author: Ligonier Ministries
D4.work: Mephibosheth Sits at the King’s Table

reflections.title: The Kindness of God

reflect.text: Mephibosheth living far away in exile is a clear picture of our own spiritual condition before God. We were completely helpless and separated from Him, unable to save ourselves or improve our state. Yet just as David brought Mephibosheth into his palace, God took the initiative to search for us. Through Jesus Christ, God extends His unmerited grace, giving us kindness that we did not earn. When we realize how generously God has reached out to rescue us, we are moved to actively show that same mercy to the people around us.

questions: How does David actively searching for someone to bless challenge how you treat people who might disagree with you?
How does remembering your own helpless state before God change the way you view others who need mercy?
reflections.prayer: Lord God, thank You for seeking us out when we were lost and helpless in our sin. You did not treat us with judgment, but showered us with Your free grace through Jesus Christ. Help us to share that same mercy and eager kindness with everyone we meet. Amen.

D5.author: Michael Youssef, Ph.D.
D5.work: Receiving the Unmerited Favor of God

unsupported.text: In 2 Samuel 9, King David asked if anyone was left from Saul's family so that he could show them the kindness of God. Kings in the ancient world commonly wiped out rival families to secure their own reign. Instead of seeking revenge or punishment, David actively went looking for someone he could bless. His inquiry led him to find Mephibosheth hiding far away in Lo-debar, helpless and lame in both feet.
unsupported.problem: Neither the passage nor the devotional states that ancient kings commonly wiped out rival families to secure their reign, nor that Mephibosheth was hiding in Lo-debar.
